Why LLM reinforcement learning breaks on robots, and how the frontier is fixing it

Why is reinforcement learning on robots so much harder than on language models, and why can't we reuse the LLM recipe? An LLM picks from a finite menu of tokens, so it gets the exact probability of each answer for free. A robot outputs continuous actions from a flow policy, which gives classical RL neither that probability nor a stable gradient through the critic. This review explains those constraints and how RECAP, π0.7, GVC, DSRL and QF3 work around them, and it ends with possible future directions.

October 27, 202632 min read

reinforcement-learningrobot-learningflow-matchingfoundation-models

Whole board

I dug into this because I wanted to understand why reinforcement learning struggles with flow matching: repeatedly refining noise into robot actions. Why is getting it to improve such a headache?

The language-model recipe makes this look straightforward. Give the model a prompt, sample 64 answers, score them, and increase the probability of answers that beat the group's average. That's GRPO, one of the methods behind LLM progress in math and code. Its older sibling, PPO, trained the first chat models.

A modern robot policy even looks familiar: a pretrained vision-language transformer with a small action head. We call it a VLA, for vision-language-action model. Same transformer, similar pretraining. So let's take a Unitree G1 humanoid with 29 joints, ask it to fold a shirt, and send motor commands 50 times a second (50 Hz). Where does the LLM recipe come apart?

The two standard policy-gradient routes need different things. PPO and GRPO need the exact log-probability of a sampled action. SAC needs to differentiate a critic's score, its prediction of future reward, back through the policy. A flow policy makes the first expensive to compute and the second unstable. A third route starts with behavior cloning (BC), supervised learning that copies recorded actions, and adds the reward as an input.

Robots trigger the whole deadly triad

Part of the difficulty is that a real robot needs all three ingredients of the deadly triad: function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data. Together, these can make value learning blow up. Toy problems can often drop one; the robot has a reason to keep every one.

Function approximation. A humanoid like Figure 02 or the G1 has 23 to 43 continuous degrees of freedom (DoF, the joints you can command), plus camera images. Try making a table with a row for every combination of 43 joint angles and every possible image. We need neural networks that generalize from states in the data to states the robot hasn't seen.

Bootstrapping. At 50 Hz, folding a shirt or busing a table takes thousands of frames. We could wait until the end and assign the final score to every frame. But thousands of random decisions contributed to that score. Which ones helped? The estimate for any individual decision is very noisy. Instead, we train on the immediate reward rrr plus the critic's predicted return V(s′)V(s')V(s′) from the next state s′s's′, discounted by γ\gammaγ, a factor just below 1:

r+γV(s′)r + \gamma V(s') r+γV(s′)

This is bootstrapping. The target contains the critic's own guess, so its errors feed into its next round of training.

Off-policy replay. Robot hours cost money. Motors heat up, parts break, and someone has to reset the objects after each attempt. Spending a rollout on one gradient step and discarding it is painful. We want a replay buffer that keeps teaching us from old trajectories: human demonstrations, autonomous successes, near-misses and failures. This is off-policy learning, because the data can come from policies other than the one we're currently training.

Why not copy LLM RL?

Simulation lets us separate the flow-policy problem from the cost of collecting robot data. Train a G1 to walk in Isaac Gym with 4,096 parallel environments, and rollouts are cheap. One attempt fails, 4,095 others keep running, and resets are instant. PPO works very well here.

The walking policy helps. It's a small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that outputs a mean and a spread for each joint. Sample the torque from that unimodal Gaussian bell, and its log-probability costs one line of math. I'll write this as log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)logπθ​(a∣s): the log-probability that policy π\piπ, with weights θ\thetaθ, selects action aaa in state sss. PPO and GRPO can both use it directly.

Dexterous manipulation with a VLA like π0\pi_0π0​ introduces two problems.

  1. The math wall, even in simulation. Manipulation needs several good answers to coexist. A flow-matching policy, a cousin of diffusion, can represent them by repeatedly refining random noise into an action a1a_1a1​. But the resulting log⁡πθ(a1∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a_1 \mid s)logπθ​(a1​∣s) has no closed form. PPO and GRPO lose the number their loss needs before we even touch a real robot.
  2. The reset and replay wall, in the real world. GRPO compares 64 answers to the same prompt. An LLM can copy that prompt 64 times in GPU memory, giving every attempt an identical starting state and a fair group-average baseline without a critic. Try restoring a crumpled shirt to exactly the same wrinkles 64 times. A robot deployed in someone's home also can't stop and collect fresh on-policy rollouts for every update. It needs to learn from whatever has accumulated in replay.

I contribute to Hugging Face's LeRobot, which is where this gap first caught my attention. Open source has good imitation learners, including π0\pi_0π0​ and ACT, alongside a 2018-era SAC. The 2025 to 2026 off-policy generative RL stack we'll look at here is still missing.

The route

I'll separate the RL update from the flow policy, then put them together to see where the trouble starts.

  1. Section 1 derives the two classic gradient families from the product rule. Score-function methods increase the probability of sampled actions that did well. Pathwise methods climb the critic's slope, giving us Q-learning for continuous actions. Each needs something different from the policy.
  2. Section 2 explains why the robot needs two good answers at once, and how flow matching in π0\pi_0π0​ produces them.
  3. Section 3 follows both gradients through the flow and shows where each becomes difficult.
  4. Section 4 develops family 3: condition the policy on the reward and train with BC. This covers RECAP, π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ and GVC, a generative value classifier.
  5. Section 5 develops family 4: search among realistic motions, the manifold of real data, by steering a frozen flow or tilting its velocity. It ends with the experiment I'd like to run next.

The side board follows the text as you scroll. Its first panel maps the four families, from REINFORCE in 1992 to π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​, GVC and QF3 in 2026.

1. Score-function versus pathwise gradients

The cliff paradox

To see what RL needs from the policy, let's first give the robot one joint so we can draw both update directions. Its action aaa is one number, say a wrist torque.

Our critic Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s, a)Qϕ​(s,a), a network with weights ϕ\phiϕ, predicts the return, meaning total future reward, from taking aaa in state sss. On the board its curve peaks at a=+1.5a = +1.5a=+1.5, with a return of 8, then falls off a cliff just past a=+2.0a = +2.0a=+2.0. Push the wrist too far and the cup leaves the table.

The policy is a Gaussian centered at μθ=0\mu_\theta = 0μθ​=0. The critic reads 2 there, roughly what the policy currently earns, so we'll use V(s)=2V(s) = 2V(s)=2 as the baseline.

Now suppose we sample a=+2.0a = +2.0a=+2.0. The critic gives it 7. Compared with the baseline, this is a good action. Its advantage, how much better it is than average, is

A=Qϕ(s,2.0)−V(s)=7−2=+5A = Q_\phi(s, 2.0) - V(s) = 7 - 2 = +5 A=Qϕ​(s,2.0)−V(s)=7−2=+5

But a=2.0a = 2.0a=2.0 is already past the peak. The slope there is negative, ∂Qϕ/∂a<0\partial Q_\phi / \partial a < 0∂Qϕ​/∂a<0. Moving right lowers the return and brings us closer to the cliff.

Which way should we move the Gaussian?

PPO sees the advantage of +5 and makes +2.0 more likely, moving the bell right. SAC sees the negative slope and moves left, toward the peak at +1.5.

For a fixed critic, the underlying score-function and pathwise estimators are unbiased estimates of the same gradient. They agree when averaged over many samples. This one sample sends them in opposite directions because one measures how good the action was, while the other measures which way improves it.

Family 1: score-function gradients (REINFORCE, PPO, GRPO)

We want policy weights θ\thetaθ that increase expected return. First pretend the wrist has a finite menu of torques. Then expected return J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ) is a sum over the actions:

J(θ)=∑aπθ(a∣s) Q(s,a)J(\theta) = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, Q(s, a) J(θ)=a∑​πθ​(a∣s)Q(s,a)

Every term multiplies how often we choose aaa by how much it earns. Apply the product rule, (u⋅v)′=u′v+uv′(u \cdot v)' = u'v + uv'(u⋅v)′=u′v+uv′:

∇θJ(θ)=∑a[(∇θπθ(a∣s)) Q(s,a)+πθ(a∣s) ∇θQ(s,a)⏟= 0]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \sum_a \Big[\big(\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\big)\, Q(s, a) + \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \underbrace{\nabla_\theta Q(s, a)}_{=\,0}\Big] ∇θ​J(θ)=a∑​[(∇θ​πθ​(a∣s))Q(s,a)+πθ​(a∣s)=0∇θ​Q(s,a)​​]

Each action in this sum is fixed. Changing θ\thetaθ changes how often we choose +2.0; with the critic held fixed, it doesn't change the score assigned to +2.0. Only the first term survives.

For continuous actions, summing over the whole axis becomes an integral. We'd like an expectation we can estimate with a few samples. Multiply and divide by πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a \mid s)πθ​(a∣s), then use the log derivative, ∇θπθ/πθ=∇θlog⁡πθ\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta / \pi_\theta = \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta∇θ​πθ​/πθ​=∇θ​logπθ​:

∇θJ(θ)=∑aπθ(a∣s) ∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s) Q(s,a)=Ea∼πθ[A(s,a) ∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, Q(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[A(s, a)\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\Big] ∇θ​J(θ)=a∑​πθ​(a∣s)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)Q(s,a)=Ea∼πθ​​[A(s,a)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)]

I also replaced QQQ with A(s,a)=Q(s,a)−V(s)A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s)A(s,a)=Q(s,a)−V(s). Subtracting a state baseline leaves the expectation unchanged because Ea∼πθ[∇θlog⁡πθ]=0\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta] = 0Ea∼πθ​​[∇θ​logπθ​]=0. It reduces variance: ordinary actions get an advantage near zero, and unusually good or bad actions get a stronger update.

This log-derivative trick underlies REINFORCE (1992), PPO (2017) and GRPO (2024). You can read it as supervised learning: use the sampled action as the label, compute the gradient that makes it more likely, and multiply by the advantage. A positive advantage encourages the action. A negative one discourages it.

For our Gaussian, the log-probability gradient with respect to its mean is

∂log⁡π∂μ=a−μσ2\frac{\partial \log \pi}{\partial \mu} = \frac{a - \mu}{\sigma^2} ∂μ∂logπ​=σ2a−μ​

Here σ\sigmaσ is the spread. At a=2.0a = 2.0a=2.0, μ=0\mu = 0μ=0, this derivative is positive. Multiply by A=+5A = +5A=+5 and the mean moves right. The calculation never asked about the critic's slope.

Why PPO wins in simulation and flatlines on an old buffer

Avoiding the slope is useful when rollouts are cheap. Our cliff drawing supplied a QQQ curve to compare the two gradients. Ordinary PPO estimates advantages from actual rollouts using a state critic Vϕ(s)V_\phi(s)Vϕ​(s) trained on fresh data. Its actor never climbs an action critic's slope ∇aQϕ\nabla_a Q_\phi∇a​Qϕ​.

An action critic can predict a huge return somewhere nobody has tried an action. I'll call that unsupported spike a critic mirage. PPO avoids these action-space mirages because it doesn't query untried actions.

Replay brings a different problem. PPO compares the current policy with πold\pi_{\text{old}}πold​, the policy that collected the sample, using their probability ratio:

r(θ)=πθ(a∣s)πold(a∣s)r(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)} r(θ)=πold​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)​

A ratio of 1.5 means the action is now 50% more likely. PPO uses a clip at [0.8,1.2][0.8, 1.2][0.8,1.2] to limit the incentive to move further. Its objective for one sample is

L(θ)=min⁡(rA, clip(r,0.8,1.2) A)L(\theta) = \min\big(r A,\ \text{clip}(r, 0.8, 1.2)\, A\big) L(θ)=min(rA, clip(r,0.8,1.2)A)

For A>0A > 0A>0, the objective increases with rrr until 1.2, then flattens. For A<0A < 0A<0, it is flat below 0.8. Once a sample reaches the flat side, making a good action more likely or a bad action less likely earns nothing further. Its gradient is zero.

Fresh data starts with ratios at 1, which is where this clip is useful. Now take a buffer from 3 days ago. Training has moved the policy, so old samples can have ratios far outside [0.8,1.2][0.8, 1.2][0.8,1.2]. Those on the plateaus contribute zero gradient. We kept the expensive robot experience, but this PPO update gets nothing from it.

Where Q-learning sits, and family 2: pathwise gradients (DDPG, TD3, SAC)

Discrete Q-learning, including DQN, can dispense with an actor. With KKK game buttons, evaluate every button and choose a∗=arg⁡max⁡aQϕ(s,a)a^* = \arg\max_a Q_\phi(s, a)a∗=argmaxa​Qϕ​(s,a). A handful of Atari buttons makes this easy.

The G1 has ∞29\infty^{29}∞29 combinations of continuous joint commands. We need a network to find the maximum for us. That network is the actor aθ(s)a_\theta(s)aθ​(s), trained to climb ∇aQϕ(s,a)\nabla_a Q_\phi(s, a)∇a​Qϕ​(s,a). This is continuous Q-learning with an amortized argmax: we pay for the search during training, then produce an action in one forward pass.

A stochastic policy also gives us exploration and multiple possible futures. Jiggling a torque helps discover better actions; sampling different futures lets us go left or right around an obstacle.

To differentiate through that sampling, we use the reparameterization trick, also used in variational autoencoders (VAEs). Writing a∼N(μθ,σθ2)a \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_\theta^2)a∼N(μθ​,σθ2​) leaves the dependence of the sampled action on θ\thetaθ hidden inside a random draw. Instead, draw parameter-free noise ϵ∼N(0,I)\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)ϵ∼N(0,I) and write

aθ(s,ϵ)=μθ(s)+σθ(s) ϵa_\theta(s, \epsilon) = \mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\, \epsilon aθ​(s,ϵ)=μθ​(s)+σθ​(s)ϵ

The identity matrix III gives independent coordinates with unit spread. The action distribution stays the same, but for a fixed noise draw the action is now a smooth function of θ\thetaθ.

Average over the noise density p(ϵ)=N(0,I)p(\epsilon) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)p(ϵ)=N(0,I) and differentiate. Here NweightsN_{\text{weights}}Nweights​ counts the actor's weights:

J(θ)=Eϵ∼p(ϵ)[Qϕ(s,aθ(s,ϵ))]  ⟹  ∇θJ(θ)=Eϵ∼p(ϵ)[∂Qϕ(s,a)∂a∣a=aθ⏟1×29⋅∇θaθ(s,ϵ)⏟29×Nweights]J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim p(\epsilon)}\Big[Q_\phi\big(s, a_\theta(s, \epsilon)\big)\Big] \implies \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim p(\epsilon)}\Big[\underbrace{\frac{\partial Q_\phi(s, a)}{\partial a}\Big|_{a = a_\theta}}_{1 \times 29} \cdot \underbrace{\nabla_\theta a_\theta(s, \epsilon)}_{29 \times N_{\text{weights}}}\Big] J(θ)=Eϵ∼p(ϵ)​[Qϕ​(s,aθ​(s,ϵ))]⟹∇θ​J(θ)=Eϵ∼p(ϵ)​[1×29∂a∂Qϕ​(s,a)​​a=aθ​​​​⋅29×Nweights​∇θ​aθ​(s,ϵ)​​]

The product-rule term containing ∇θp(ϵ)\nabla_\theta p(\epsilon)∇θ​p(ϵ) vanishes because the noise density has no θ\thetaθ in it.

The shapes on the board help. The critic supplies 29 slopes, one per joint. Each slope gives a direction and a steepness. The actor Jacobian, a 29×Nweights29 \times N_{\text{weights}}29×Nweights​ matrix of derivatives, tells us how each weight moves each joint. Their product gives one gradient over the actor's weights. This is how SAC moves left in the cliff picture.

The cost appears in the loop below it:

  1. Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s, a)Qϕ​(s,a) grows a spike at an action the data never covered.
  2. The actor climbs ∇aQϕ\nabla_a Q_\phi∇a​Qϕ​ toward that mirage.
  3. The Bellman backup y=r+γQϕ(s′,aθ(s′))y = r + \gamma Q_\phi\big(s', a_\theta(s')\big)y=r+γQϕ​(s′,aθ​(s′)) uses the inflated next-state value to train earlier states.

The error spreads backward through the data, drawing more states toward the same false peak. This is the deadly triad at work.

The classic algorithms add protections:

  • DDPG (2015) gives us the basic loop.
  • TD3 (2018) trains twin critics and backs up min⁡(Q1,Q2)\min(Q_1, Q_2)min(Q1​,Q2​). A random spike rarely shows up in both critics at the same action, so the other vetoes it. It also updates the actor less often, giving the critics time to correct errors before the actor follows them.
  • SAC (2018) keeps a stochastic Gaussian and adds an entropy bonus −αlog⁡πθ-\alpha \log \pi_\theta−αlogπθ​, weighted by α\alphaα. It rewards uncertainty. Without that pressure, σθ\sigma_\thetaσθ​ collapses toward 0 at a peak, where ∇aQϕ=0\nabla_a Q_\phi = 0∇a​Qϕ​=0, and exploration stops.

What each family needs from the policy

We can now state what the policy has to provide.

Family 1: score-function Family 2: pathwise
Gradient A⋅∇θlog⁡πθA \cdot \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\thetaA⋅∇θ​logπθ​ ∇aQϕ⋅∇θaθ\nabla_a Q_\phi \cdot \nabla_\theta a_\theta∇a​Qϕ​⋅∇θ​aθ​
Needs an exact log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)logπθ​(a∣s) a short differentiable path from θ\thetaθ to aaa

The robot wants replay efficiency without chasing mirages. Unfortunately, a flow policy has no closed-form log⁡πθ\log \pi_\thetalogπθ​, and its action gradient must cross every refinement step. Before following those gradients, we need to understand why we'd choose this policy in the first place.

2. Multimodality versus tractable likelihoods

The mug in the way

Our G1 reaches past a coffee mug. Half the demonstrations go left, a=−1a = -1a=−1, and half go right, a=+1a = +1a=+1. Both work.

Fit a unimodal Gaussian MLP to these demonstrations with squared error, and its center goes to their average, a=0a = 0a=0. Straight into the mug. We need a policy that keeps left and right as separate answers.

An LLM's discrete softmax handles this easily. Suppose it has 1,024 token bins. Their probabilities obey

∑k=11024πθ(k∣s)=1\sum_{k=1}^{1024} \pi_\theta(k \mid s) = 1 k=1∑1024​πθ​(k∣s)=1

The softmax converts raw scores, or logits, into probabilities. Increase the correct token's logit and the denominator grows, reducing the probabilities of the other 1,023 tokens. Cross-entropy, the usual classification loss, therefore supplies contrast automatically. Its gradient on each logit is π(k∣s)−1\pi(k \mid s) - 1π(k∣s)−1 for the correct token and π(k∣s)\pi(k \mid s)π(k∣s) for each wrong token.

Two good bins can both hold probability mass. We also get an exact log⁡πθ\log \pi_\thetalogπθ​ in one forward pass. Physical Intelligence's FAST brings this machinery to robot actions: it compresses continuous action chunks with a JPEG-style discrete cosine transform and converts them into discrete tokens.

Flow matching gives us another way to keep several answers. Its regression loss pulls toward recorded actions, with no automatic softmax-style suppression of wrong answers elsewhere. Later, we'll use reward labels to recover that contrast.

Flow matching: iterative test-time thinking

For π0\pi_0π0​, the output a1a_1a1​ is a whole action chunk: targets for all 29 joints over the next 50 control steps. That's 50×29=1,45050 \times 29 = 1{,}45050×29=1,450 continuous numbers. These are ticks of the robot's 50 Hz clock. As it moves, the policy recomputes chunks and merges overlapping ones.

Flow matching and diffusion spend iterative test-time compute on this continuous output. Call the same network K=10K = 10K=10 times, starting with noise a0a_0a0​ and progressively refining it into a1a_1a1​.

The network predicts a velocity vθ(at,t,s)v_\theta(a_t, t, s)vθ​(at​,t,s). Its inputs are a partly finished chunk ata_tat​, the state sss, and sampler time ttt, running from noise at 0 to a finished chunk at 1. This clock is separate from the robot's 50 Hz clock. Each sampler step updates all 1,450 numbers.

Training uses the replay buffer:

  1. Take a recorded chunk a1a_1a1​.
  2. Draw matching noise a0∼N(0,I)a_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)a0​∼N(0,I).
  3. Choose t∈[0,1]t \in [0, 1]t∈[0,1] and interpolate: at=(1−t) a0+t a1a_t = (1 - t)\, a_0 + t\, a_1at​=(1−t)a0​+ta1​.
  4. Train the velocity at that point to match the full displacement a1−a0a_1 - a_0a1​−a0​.

This self-supervised regression is conditional flow matching (CFM):

LCFM(θ)=Et,a0,a1[∥vθ(at,t,s)−(a1−a0)∥2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, a_0, a_1}\Big[\big\| v_\theta(a_t, t, s) - (a_1 - a_0) \big\|^2\Big] LCFM​(θ)=Et,a0​,a1​​[​vθ​(at​,t,s)−(a1​−a0​)​2]

Training and sampling look like this:

# train: one step on a batch of B recorded chunks
a1 = buffer.sample_chunks()   # (B, 50, 29)
a0 = randn_like(a1)           # noise
t  = rand(B, 1, 1)            # per-sample time in [0, 1]
at = (1 - t) * a0 + t * a1    # a point on the line
loss = ((v(at, t, s) - (a1 - a0)) ** 2).mean()

# act: 10 Euler steps from noise to a chunk
a = randn(50, 29)
for k in range(10):
    a = a + 0.1 * v(a, k / 10, s)

I had to pause over the target at t=0.9t = 0.9t=0.9. We've nearly arrived, yet we're still asking for the whole arrow a1−a0a_1 - a_0a1​−a0​. Why doesn't this overshoot?

Because the target is a velocity. Think of vθv_\thetavθ​ as a speedometer. On a 60-mile road traveled in 1 hour, it reads 60 mph at t=0t = 0t=0, 0.50.50.5 and 0.90.90.9. At mile 54, the last step lasts only Δt=0.1\Delta t = 0.1Δt=0.1 hour, so 54+0.1×60=6054 + 0.1 \times 60 = 6054+0.1×60=60. The code's a + 0.1 * v does the same speed-times-time calculation.

A constant-velocity target has the same size at every ttt, so the gradients never vanish near t=1t = 1t=1.

But why take 10 steps if the training paths are straight lines? Couldn't we jump the whole way?

Look at the upper drawing. Noise samples at t=0t = 0t=0 are paired with either a1=−1a_1 = -1a1​=−1 or a1=+1a_1 = +1a1​=+1. Near the start, training lines headed both ways cross. Squared-error regression averages their arrows. At t=0t = 0t=0, one big step takes each sample to the average target, the mug.

The lower drawing shows the new paths produced during sampling. With small 0.1 vθ0.1\,v_\theta0.1vθ​ steps, we ask for a fresh velocity after every move. A particle that moves right enters a region with more right-bound training lines; its next arrow turns further right. Repeating this splits the samples into two branches around the mug, even though the individual training pairs were straight.

3. Why flow matching breaks both standard RL families

Now we can follow the two RL calculations through those ten steps. For the score-function update, we need the final chunk's log-probability. For the pathwise update, we need the critic's slope to reach the policy weights.

The first calculation tracks how the flow squeezes probability. The second multiplies derivatives through the sampler.

Family 1 breaks: squeezed volume and the Jacobian trace

Take a one-dimensional slice of noise with width Δa0=1.0\Delta a_0 = 1.0Δa0​=1.0 containing 30% of the probability mass. Suppose the flow squeezes it into width Δa1=0.01\Delta a_1 = 0.01Δa1​=0.01. The mass stays 30%, so its density rises from 0.3/1.0=0.30.3 / 1.0 = 0.30.3/1.0=0.3 to 0.3/0.01=300.3 / 0.01 = 300.3/0.01=30. A 100× increase.

Knowing the starting Gaussian density isn't enough. We have to account for that squeezing along the entire path.

The sampler approximates an ordinary differential equation (ODE), dat/dt=vθ(at,t,s)da_t/dt = v_\theta(a_t, t, s)dat​/dt=vθ​(at​,t,s). In one dimension, ∂v/∂a\partial v / \partial a∂v/∂a gives the local stretching rate. Negative means points ahead move slower than those behind, compressing the slice. Positive means it stretches.

With multiple coordinates, the rate is the divergence: the sum of diagonal entries, or trace, of the Jacobian ∂vθ/∂at\partial v_\theta / \partial a_t∂vθ​/∂at​. This matrix records how every velocity coordinate changes with every position coordinate. Each diagonal entry gives one coordinate's stretching rate.

To keep the drawing small, use one 29-joint action. The Jacobian is 29×2929 \times 2929×29; for our full chunk it would be 1,450×1,4501{,}450 \times 1{,}4501,450×1,450. Starting from known Gaussian density p0p_0p0​, the continuous-flow likelihood is

log⁡πθ(a1∣s)=log⁡p0(a0)−∫01(∑i=129∂vθ,i(at,t,s)∂at,i)dt\log \pi_\theta(a_1 \mid s) = \log p_0(a_0) - \int_0^1 \left(\sum_{i=1}^{29} \frac{\partial v_{\theta,i}(a_t, t, s)}{\partial a_{t,i}}\right) dt logπθ​(a1​∣s)=logp0​(a0​)−∫01​(i=1∑29​∂at,i​∂vθ,i​(at​,t,s)​)dt

Here vθ,iv_{\theta,i}vθ,i​ is coordinate iii's velocity. The 10 Euler steps approximate this continuous path. For our one-dimensional slice, the divergence integral is ln⁡(Δa1/Δa0)=ln⁡0.01≈−4.6\ln(\Delta a_1 / \Delta a_0) = \ln 0.01 \approx -4.6ln(Δa1​/Δa0​)=ln0.01≈−4.6. Subtracting it increases log density by 4.6, or density by e4.6≈100e^{4.6} \approx 100e4.6≈100.

So there is a likelihood calculation. It's just expensive. One backward pass supplies one Jacobian row, and each diagonal entry needs a different row. Even the 29-joint version takes 29 backward passes at each of 10 ODE steps, for every sample. PPO then differentiates this calculation again with respect to θ\thetaθ. At VLA scale, that is intractable.

What if we constrain the Jacobian?

We can make likelihoods easier by constraining the flow. SAC-NF (arXiv:1905.06893), NFPO (arXiv:2603.11470), PrT-Flow (arXiv:2610.17667) and GenPO++ (arXiv:2606.06967) use triangular Jacobians or reversible flows. Spectral normalization can instead bound the Jacobian to make the flow Lipschitz (arXiv:2504.08246). Triangular or bi-Lipschitz Jacobians restrict each layer's expressiveness (arXiv:2107.07232), however, and exclude standard unconstrained transformer action experts such as π0\pi_0π0​'s.

Family 2 breaks: ten Jacobians multiply into a mirage

We could skip likelihoods and backpropagate the critic's slope through the differentiable sampler. Write its first two Euler steps:

a0.1=a0+0.1 vθ(a0,0,s),a0.2=a0.1+0.1 vθ(a0.1,0.1,s)a_{0.1} = a_0 + 0.1\, v_\theta(a_0, 0, s), \qquad a_{0.2} = a_{0.1} + 0.1\, v_\theta(a_{0.1}, 0.1, s) a0.1​=a0​+0.1vθ​(a0​,0,s),a0.2​=a0.1​+0.1vθ​(a0.1​,0.1,s)

Step 1's output becomes step 2's input. All ten form nested functions, f10(f9(…f1(a0)))f_{10}(f_9(\dots f_1(a_0)))f10​(f9​(…f1​(a0​))), whose Jacobians multiply in the backward pass.

The same θ\thetaθ appears at every step. Follow its contribution from step 1: that contribution must cross nine subsequent steps to reach the critic. For tk=k/10t_k = k/10tk​=k/10, its sampled gradient is

g1=∂Qϕ(s,a1)∂a1⋅J9J8⋯J1⋅∂a0.1∂θ,Jk=I+0.1 ∂vθ(atk,tk,s)∂atkg_1 = \frac{\partial Q_\phi(s, a_1)}{\partial a_1} \cdot J_9 J_8 \cdots J_1 \cdot \frac{\partial a_{0.1}}{\partial \theta}, \qquad J_k = I + 0.1\, \frac{\partial v_\theta(a_{t_k}, t_k, s)}{\partial a_{t_k}} g1​=∂a1​∂Qϕ​(s,a1​)​⋅J9​J8​⋯J1​⋅∂θ∂a0.1​​,Jk​=I+0.1∂atk​​∂vθ​(atk​​,tk​,s)​

Each JkJ_kJk​ contains the identity III, carrying the chunk forward, plus the velocity network's correction. The full gradient sums ten contributions like this, one from each step.

We've built backpropagation through a 10-layer recurrent neural network (RNN). If the nine factors each stretch a direction by 1.3, it grows by 1.39≈10.61.3^9 \approx 10.61.39≈10.6. Scale it by 0.7 each time and it shrinks to 0.79≈0.040.7^9 \approx 0.040.79≈0.04. Different directions can explode or vanish.

The signal being transformed is the critic's slope in 1,450 dimensions. Coordinated robot motions occupy a thin manifold in that space. Most arbitrary combinations of 1,450 numbers resemble no recorded motion, and the critic has no data there. An amplified slope can steer the policy off the motion manifold toward a critic mirage. The same error loop we drew earlier now sits behind ten stages of amplification.

4. Family 3: condition the policy on the reward

Patching PPO onto flows: πRL and FPO

One approach keeps PPO and changes how the flow supplies its likelihood.

πRL, following DPPO, adds noise to every denoising step. The initial noise already makes the final chunk random, but once it's drawn, the Euler steps are deterministic. Treating a deterministic step as a Gaussian gives σ=0\sigma = 0σ=0, which breaks the Gaussian log-probability calculation.

Inject Gaussian noise into all 10 steps and each becomes a small Gaussian policy with an exact log-probability. We can treat the denoising process as additional steps of a Markov decision process (MDP) and apply PPO.

This extends the credit-assignment problem. An episode with 50 robot decisions and 10 denoising steps per decision becomes 50×10=50050 \times 10 = 50050×10=500 steps. The reward still arrives at the end.

FPO keeps the deterministic flow and substitutes a proxy. It uses the change in flow-matching loss to estimate the change in log⁡πθ\log \pi_\thetalogπθ​: a lower regression loss roughly indicates higher likelihood. This comes from an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on log-likelihood. The estimated ratio then goes into PPO's [0.8,1.2][0.8, 1.2][0.8,1.2] clip.

Physical Intelligence tested FPO and PPO on real-robot laundry folding in Appendix D of the π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ paper (arXiv:2511.14759). The noisy flow-loss proxy failed to track how far the policy had moved. The clip didn't trigger, updates damaged the pretrained VLA weights, and training collapsed. Lowering the learning rate enough to stabilize it left very little improvement. On the board, the proxy needle stays inside the guardrail while the true ratio has already crossed it.

RECAP (π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​): the reward becomes an input

Condition the policy on the reward. We already know how to train a flow with BC, using ∥vθ−(a1−a0)∥2\|v_\theta - (a_1 - a_0)\|^2∥vθ​−(a1​−a0​)∥2. Keep that loss and add a label describing how well the trajectory went. We never differentiate through the reward.

RECAP does this in three steps:

  1. Train a state critic Vϕ(s)V_\phi(s)Vϕ​(s) offline. It predicts a distribution over 201 value bins instead of one scalar. It scores states in the buffer, avoiding queries about untried actions and their mirages.
  2. Use the critic to label the buffer's trajectories by advantage. The top 30% get I=GoodI = \text{Good}I=Good; the rest get I=BadI = \text{Bad}I=Bad.
  3. Train with plain, unweighted BC, supplying the label as an input:

LRECAP(θ)=∥vθ(at,t,s,I)−(a1−a0)∥2\mathcal{L}_{\text{RECAP}}(\theta) = \big\| v_\theta(a_t, t, s, I) - (a_1 - a_0) \big\|^2 LRECAP​(θ)=​vθ​(at​,t,s,I)−(a1​−a0​)​2

The label acts like an LLM prompt: one network learns both behaviors, and at test time we request the one we want.

Keeping the bad trajectories serves two purposes. First, they still teach representations. Advantage-weighted regression (AWR), the standard reward-weighted BC approach, multiplies each squared error by w=eA/βw = e^{A/\beta}w=eA/β, with temperature β\betaβ. Those weights must stay positive: a negative weight rewards increasing the error, sending ∥vθ∥→∞\|v_\theta\| \to \infty∥vθ​∥→∞. Bad samples therefore receive tiny weights, and in practice AWR discards 80 to 90% of the buffer's effective contribution.

RECAP keeps 100% of the trajectories at weight 1.0. The VLA learns to separate successful and failed motions across all the physical states in the data.

Second, the mixed data enables classifier-free guidance (CFG). At each sampler step, query the same network twice: once without the label, giving vallv_{\text{all}}vall​, and once with Good, giving vgoodv_{\text{good}}vgood​. Dropping the label on some training steps teaches the unlabeled prediction. We need no separate classifier or critic to differentiate at test time.

The difference vgood−vallv_{\text{good}} - v_{\text{all}}vgood​−vall​ gives a direction in velocity space. If you've seen Anthropic's sparse autoencoders and activation steering, the operation may look familiar: subtract a “sycophancy” direction from an LLM's activations to change its behavior. Here, we move from the mixed velocity toward Good and away from Bad. With guidance weight β\betaβ, separate from AWR's temperature:

vguided=vall+β (vgood−vall)v_{\text{guided}} = v_{\text{all}} + \beta\, \big(v_{\text{good}} - v_{\text{all}}\big) vguided​=vall​+β(vgood​−vall​)

At β=0\beta = 0β=0 we use the mixed velocity; at 1 we use Good; above 1 we extrapolate past it.

The mixture depends on which class is likely to have produced the current point, so its weights vary across the flow. At the board's point, suppose they match the dataset's 30% Good and 70% Bad. Let vgood=(0.7,1)v_{\text{good}} = (0.7, 1)vgood​=(0.7,1) and vbad=(−0.3,1)v_{\text{bad}} = (-0.3, 1)vbad​=(−0.3,1). Then

vall=0.3 (0.7,1)+0.7 (−0.3,1)=(0,1)v_{\text{all}} = 0.3\,(0.7, 1) + 0.7\,(-0.3, 1) = (0, 1) vall​=0.3(0.7,1)+0.7(−0.3,1)=(0,1)

The difference vector is (0.7,0)(0.7, 0)(0.7,0). Set β=2\beta = 2β=2:

vguided=(0,1)+2 (0.7,0)=(1.4,1)v_{\text{guided}} = (0, 1) + 2\,(0.7, 0) = (1.4, 1) vguided​=(0,1)+2(0.7,0)=(1.4,1)

We move twice as far sideways as the Good velocity, pushing further away from the failure modes. The implementation still uses ordinary flow-matching regression:

# label once, with the 201-bin state critic V
for traj in buffer:
    good = advantage(V, traj) in top_30_percent
    traj.I = "Good" if good else "Bad"

# train: plain flow-matching BC on 100% of the data,
# with the label as an input
# (dropping I on some steps teaches the unlabeled v_all)
loss = ((v(at, t, s, I) - (a1 - a0)) ** 2).mean()

# act: two network calls per Euler step
for k in range(10):
    v_all  = v(a, k / 10, s, I=None)
    v_good = v(a, k / 10, s, I="Good")
    a = a + 0.1 * (v_all + 2.0 * (v_good - v_all))

You can try this below. Each action is a 2D point where the gripper passes the mug, seen from above. The clean left and right passes make up the top 30% of demonstrations and get Good labels. A central crash and two clumsy brushes get Bad labels. The velocity field is the exact flow-matching solution for these data, what a perfect network would learn. You control Euler steps KKK and guidance β\betaβ.

Start with β=0\beta = 0β=0 and one step: every sample goes to the data average, inside the mug. Increase the steps and the samples separate into all five clusters, including the crash. Then set K=2K = 2K=2 and increase β\betaβ from 0 through 1 to 2. With the default 160 samples and seed 7, Good-only guidance at β=1\beta = 1β=1 still leaves 34% nearest a Bad cluster. At β=2\beta = 2β=2, that falls to 18%.

Richer labels (π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​) and actions in the output (GVC)

RECAP supplies one bit. π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ (arXiv:2604.15483) expands π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​'s I∈{0,1}I \in \{0, 1\}I∈{0,1} into richer metadata and a visual target:

  • Speed,
  • Quality, from 1 to 5,
  • Mistake, true or false,
  • a subgoal image showing the scene 4 s ahead.

That distills all the task specialists into one steerable generalist: you choose the behavior by choosing the labels.

The Generative Value Classifier, GVC (Swerdlow, Dong and Finn, arXiv:2610.22497), applies the same idea to value prediction. Its starting observation is that supervision comes from the output targets in the loss. A rich input supplies no extra target by itself.

A standard critic Qϕ(s,a)→R^Q_\phi(s, a) \to \hat{R}Qϕ​(s,a)→R^ receives a 1,450-D action chunk and predicts one return. Training with (R^−R)2(\hat{R} - R)^2(R^−R)2 against observed return RRR supervises one number per sample. The critic gets very little signal from all that action data.

GVC makes the return an input, represented by one of MMM bins z1,…,zMz_1, \dots, z_Mz1​,…,zM​. It predicts the action velocity:

∥vθ(at,t,s,zi)−(a1−a0)∥2\big\|v_\theta(a_t, t, s, z_i) - (a_1 - a_0)\big\|^2 ​vθ​(at​,t,s,zi​)−(a1​−a0​)​2

This is RECAP's loss with a return bin in place of Good or Bad. Each sample now supervises 1,450 output coordinates instead of 1, a 1,450× increase in the number of targets.

We still need to turn this generator into a critic. It answers “what action fits return ziz_izi​?” We want “what return fits this action?”

GVC uses Bayes' rule for Best-of-NNN selection. The policy generates N=16N = 16N=16 candidate chunks. For each candidate aaa, evaluate how well each return bin explains it, using flow-matching error as a proxy for −log⁡p(a∣s,zi)-\log p(a \mid s, z_i)−logp(a∣s,zi​). Lower error means a better explanation.

This is the ELBO-style proxy FPO used, with a smaller job: rank 16 candidates. It doesn't control the permitted size of a policy update. An action that resembles high-return behavior gets stronger support from high bins.

Combine these likelihoods with a prior p(zi∣s)p(z_i \mid s)p(zi​∣s), the return-bin probabilities before seeing the action:

p(zi∣s,a)=p(a∣s,zi) p(zi∣s)∑j=1Mp(a∣s,zj) p(zj∣s)p(z_i \mid s, a) = \frac{p(a \mid s, z_i)\, p(z_i \mid s)}{\sum_{j=1}^{M} p(a \mid s, z_j)\, p(z_j \mid s)} p(zi​∣s,a)=∑j=1M​p(a∣s,zj​)p(zj​∣s)p(a∣s,zi​)p(zi​∣s)​

The denominator normalizes across all MMM bins. Their expected value gives QGVC(s,a)=∑ip(zi∣s,a) ziQ_{\text{GVC}}(s, a) = \sum_i p(z_i \mid s, a)\, z_iQGVC​(s,a)=∑i​p(zi​∣s,a)zi​.

A temporal-difference (TD) anchor calibrates the score with (QGVC−yTD)2(Q_{\text{GVC}} - y_{\text{TD}})^2(QGVC​−yTD​)2, using the bootstrapped target yTD=r+γV(s′)y_{\text{TD}} = r + \gamma V(s')yTD​=r+γV(s′). The robot executes the highest-scoring candidate:

cands = [policy.sample(s) for _ in range(16)]

def q_gvc(a):
    # a small error means bin z explains the chunk a
    err = array([flow_error(a, s, z) for z in bins])
    # -err stands in for log p(a | s, z)
    p = softmax(-err + log_prior(s))
    return (p * bins).sum()   # expected return

execute(max(cands, key=q_gvc))

5. Beyond cloning the dataset: family 4

Breaking the behavior-cloning ceiling

RECAP and π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ learn from trajectories already in replay. Guidance and Best-of-16 steer among behaviors learned from that buffer. To improve beyond cloning and interpolating the existing trajectories, we need search driven by the critic again. How can we do that without the ten-step gradient chain and its mirages?

4A: freeze the VLA and steer it. Keep the pretrained model's weights fixed and train a small controller around it.

Policy Decorator (Yuan et al., arXiv:2412.13630), PLD (arXiv:2511.00091) and MiDAS (arXiv:2608.11363) learn a residual correction Δa\Delta aΔa added to the frozen VLA's action. A tiny network learns the edit while the VLA supplies the motion.

DSRL (Wagenmaker, Levine et al., arXiv:2506.15799) and FRS (arXiv:2606.13675) instead learn to choose the starting noise a0a_0a0​. The lightweight RL policy outputs noise, the frozen flow with weights θ\thetaθ decodes it, and the small policy learns from the return. No gradient crosses the ten ODE steps.

Each a0a_0a0​ in the Gaussian ball decodes into a realistic motion, so search stays on the learned motion manifold. Critic mirages in action space become impossible.

4B: tilt the velocity with a one-step preview. QF3 (Kim, McAllister, Goldberg, Abbeel, Kanazawa, arXiv:2610.08789) and FlowDPG (arXiv:2606.22303) keep training the flow, pulling its velocity toward the critic's slope. This builds on Q-score matching.

Recall the speed-times-time calculation. At step ttt, holding the current velocity for the remaining time gives a preview of the endpoint:

a^1=at+(1−t) vθ(at,t,s)\hat{a}_1 = a_t + (1 - t)\, v_\theta(a_t, t, s) a^1​=at​+(1−t)vθ​(at​,t,s)

Evaluate the critic's slope at a^1\hat{a}_1a^1​ and adjust the current velocity toward a better endpoint. Backpropagation crosses one step. The ten-Jacobian product never forms.

Fixing π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​'s pixel subgoals, coarse tags and amnesiac states

I see three remaining problems in π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ that point toward a more complete loop.

Pixel subgoals cost too much. Producing the image 4 s ahead takes a 14B image model 1.25 s on 4× H100. Then the policy turns the RGB image back into ViT tokens, the patch embeddings of a vision transformer. We render pixels only to re-encode them immediately. Predicting the subgoal directly in that latent ViT space skips rendering and is 100× faster.

We can still use hindsight experience replay (HER), which relabels an attempt with the goal it actually reached. Suppose our arm smoothly grabs the wrong shirt corner. The subgoal choice gets Mistake: true. For the low-level flow controller, relabel the goal as the corner it reached. It executed that motion smoothly, so it gets Quality: 5. The failed task attempt still teaches useful control.

The tags are coarse. Quality and Speed apply to whole episodes or coarse segments. A perfect grasp followed by a clumsy fold receives one tag, with no dense credit for the individual steps.

The state forgets previous attempts. Current VLAs see the current frame oto_tot​, or 2 frames. A heavy box slips from the gripper at t=1t = 1t=1 s. By t=2t = 2t=2 s it's back on the table, and the camera view matches the view before the attempt. Given the same input, the policy repeats the same failed grasp.

I'd add a compressed episodic memory-imprint vector to the state. It would encode recently tried actions and the critic's surprise ΔV\Delta VΔV, the change in predicted value when the box slipped. That gives the policy information it can use to adapt to the physics in context at test time.

The finale: simulate before you act

Max Bennett's A Brief History of Intelligence describes a leap in vertebrate brain evolution: pausing to simulate possible actions in an internal world model. Picture a cat or squirrel on a branch considering three jumps, scoring safe landings against falls, then taking the winner. LLMs have something analogous in token-level chain of thought. Physical robots have lacked the corresponding fast internal simulation and action-scoring loop.

This next part is my extrapolation. I'd combine the pieces into family 4C: propose motions, simulate them, score them and learn from the selected action. AlphaZero uses this pattern to search candidate moves with a learned value and train its policy to imitate the search.

while True:
    s = observe() + memory_imprint()
    # propose
    cands = [flow_policy.sample(s) for _ in range(16)]
    # simulate, in latent space
    future = [world_model.rollout(s, a) for a in cands]
    # score the imagined outcomes
    best = argmax([gvc_score(f) for f in future])
    # act, then distill on the next pass
    execute(cands[best])
    buffer.add(s, cands[best], quality=5)
  1. Propose. Give the multimodal flow policy the state and memory imprint. Sample N=16N = 16N=16 diverse chunks: a left grasp, a right grasp, a fast push, a gentle hook.
  2. Simulate. Roll the 16 chunks forward in a fast latent world model, in embedding space, in milliseconds. Score the imagined outcomes in parallel with GVC.
  3. Act and distill. Execute the best chunk and add its winning trajectory to replay as a new Quality: 5 experience. On the next training pass, the flow absorbs the result into its reflexes, just as AlphaZero's policy imitates search-selected moves.

Several parts already exist:

  • GPC (Qi et al., arXiv:2502.00622) samples actions from a frozen diffusion policy, forecasts them with an action-conditioned world model, and executes the best.
  • FOREWARN (Wu et al., arXiv:2502.01828) imagines plans in a latent world model and uses a fine-tuned vision-language model to select them.
  • VeriVLA (Sun et al., arXiv:2610.21985) ranks flow-VLA action chunks using task progress predicted by a latent world model of future image embeddings.
  • Ctrl-World (Guo et al., arXiv:2510.10125) and Verify, Act, Distill (Hiratsuka et al., arXiv:2610.14885) add distillation, fine-tuning with ordinary flow-matching loss on imagined successes or verifier-selected chunks.

I haven't found a paper combining GVC scores on imagined latent futures, a memory imprint in the state, and distillation of every winner back into the flow. That's the experiment I'd run next.
